explain.say: In 2022 scientists read the DNA in teeth from graves near Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan, where gravestones from 1338 and 1339 mention a pestilence. They found the plague germ, Yersinia pestis. A few years later it would kill tens of millions across Asia, the Middle East, North Africa and Europe. Look at the chain of how it travelled.

explain.say: Follow the map. Along trade routes it reached the Black Sea by 1346. Genoese ships carried it to Constantinople, then Sicily in October 1347, Alexandria and Cairo, and on to Paris and London by 1348. Fleas on rats spread the bubonic form, and the lung form spread person to person. Why did trade make the plague so fast?

explain.say: The toll was staggering: perhaps a third to a half of Europe's people, and similar losses in Egypt and Syria. In Tunis the young Ibn Khaldun lost both parents. Fear turned to hatred: Jewish communities were falsely blamed and massacred, in Strasbourg, Basel and many other places. How do you think fear makes people look for someone to blame?

explain.say: Now the consequences. See the causes on the board. With so few workers left, survivors demanded higher wages and lower rents. England's Statute of Labourers, 1351, tried to freeze wages and failed, and revolts followed, like the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Which link do you think hurt the old lords most?

faq.q: How did the Black Death spread?
faq.a: From Central Asia along trade routes to the Black Sea by 1346, then by ship to Constantinople, Egypt and Sicily in 1347, and across Europe by about 1353. DNA from graves in Kyrgyzstan dated 1338 to 1339 points to its origin there.
asks: Where did the Black Death start?

faq.q: How many people died in the Black Death?
faq.a: Estimates vary, but perhaps a third to a half of Europe's population died between 1347 and 1351, some 25 to 50 million people, with similar heavy losses in the Middle East and North Africa.
asks: What was the death toll of the Black Death?

faq.q: What was the Statute of Labourers?
faq.a: An English law of 1351, following an ordinance of 1349, that tried to hold wages at pre-plague levels and force people to work. It was hard to enforce and caused resentment.
asks: How did governments respond to the Black Death?

faq.q: What were the consequences of the Black Death?
faq.a: Labour shortages raised wages and weakened serfdom in western Europe, prompting revolts; persecution of Jewish communities; new public health measures like quarantine; and changes in religion, art and attitudes to death.
asks: How did the Black Death change Europe?

faq.q: Where does the word quarantine come from?
faq.a: From the Italian quaranta giorni, forty days. Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, ordered a thirty-day isolation for arrivals in 1377; the period was later extended to forty days.

facts: Ancient DNA has confirmed Yersinia pestis as the cause of the Black Death.
Ragusa (Dubrovnik) introduced a thirty-day isolation period in 1377.
